en: Preface to the Thirteenth Assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Section on the Perfection of Patience (*Kṣānti-pāramitā*),
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xìmíng Monastery.

Only those who possess the spiritual root of supreme enlightenment and serve as the profound masters of universal compassion can rely upon the dark ocean to benefit all beings and encompass the myriad creatures of the azure world on their far-reaching journey; therein, the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) is peerless. Thus, a circle of sublime companions gathered one after another, and divine plans were successively revealed.

To clear the obstructions of the Way and eliminate the resentment that stifles the mind, to spread kinship among the ignorant masses and open up the vast path of human feeling—though the destruction may be as severe as spears and arrows, and the harm as total as being ground to powder—one must internally purge the notion of self and externally reject the notion of others. When one perceives that even the "adjacent voids" have intervals, how could a blade cause injury?
When one contemplates that the mechanism of thought has no master, how can it be compared to touching a boat?
I have no self, so whose thing could external objects be?
It is like a great flood reaching the void; the void has no fear of drowning.
Sediment accumulates and returns to the marsh, yet the marsh itself harbors no resentment;
how much more so for sounds that have already faded— their slander and praise are of one essence—
and for complexions that have already changed— their loss and gain belong to the same category.
If one possesses great desire and abounds in pleasure, how could one further add suffering?
Without the incoming of harm, there would be no path for gathering and receiving;
without the outgoing of compassion, there would be no master for the practice of Bodhi.

On the contrary, he became a virtuous friend, and I was further moved by his profound kindness; hearing his rebukes was more delightful than the music of strings and pipes, and receiving his blows brought me greater joy than the honor of being carried on one's head.
Although the Prince lost both his eyes, he never wavered in his resolve;
only when the Rishi’s seven limbs were severed did he finally repay the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
As for its spiritual resonance and penetration: when a hundred spears converge upon the body, the signs of a hundred blessings unfold;
when ten thousand afflictions entangle the person, the foundation of ten thousand virtues is established.
As for its practical application: it reaches far back to accord with non-arising, and looking down from that realization, it distances one from the mundane world through verified purity.
From afar, they draw upon great renunciation, equalizing the left-hand side with the right-hand cutting;
when compared to the robe of shame and modesty, even the dragon-embroidered robes of an emperor do not match its splendor;
when used to ward off afflictions as armor, even the rhinoceros-hide cuirass must yield to its hardness.
When speaking of his great power, even "uprooting mountains" cannot serve as a metaphor;
when discussing his fearlessness, even "displaying valor" has no equal.
Beginning with the events and forming three [teachings], and finally proceeding through practice to establish five, all are fully based upon skillful means, and thus the Perfect Sound is manifested.
The phrasing is earnest and sincere, and the principles are meticulously examined.
This single fascicle, translated alone, is comparable to a portion of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Is this not indeed essential for the beauty of providing guidance and correction?
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Chapter Thirteen: The Section on the Perfection of Forbearance (*Kṣānti-pāramitā*). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Bhagavat was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"You should now proclaim the perfection of patience for the sake of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having received the Buddha’s instruction and being sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should deeply endure various forms of reviling, slander, and speech from other sentient beings; they should not give rise to anger, resentment, or malice, but should instead arouse loving-kindness and compassion to repay their kindness.”

In this way, a bodhisattva should have deep faith and joy in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); whatever mind of patience they may give rise to, they should dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). It is by means of this that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to abide in the perfection of patience.
Then, Śāriputra asked the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"What is the difference between the patience cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattvas and the patience cultivated by the assembly of śrāvakas?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"The patience cultivated by the assembly of śrāvakas is called the aspect of limited practice; its object of focus is not perfectly complete.
The patience cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattvas is called the aspect of comprehensive practice; its object of focus is most perfectly complete."
It refers to the immeasurable patience of bodhisattvas; desiring to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, they don the armor of patience and make this vow:
"I shall deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa."
Therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is immeasurable.

The patience of a śrāvaka is practiced solely for the sake of abandoning one's own afflictions and not for the sake of sentient beings; thus, it is called limited patience, unlike the immeasurable patience of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Because bodhisattvas do not depart from the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), it is called "patience in its full extent.

If one gives rise to impure thoughts toward a bodhisattva and fails to endure a harmful intent, know that such a person incurs immeasurable sin—not so for those of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles; therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is supreme.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas feel no anger or resentment when rebuked by a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, so too, even if they are reviled, slandered,
or defamed by those such as Caṇḍālas, Pukkasa, or other lowly sentient beings, they should not give rise to anger, malice, or the intent to retaliate for even a single kṣaṇa."
In this way, the bodhisattva’s embrace of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is swiftly brought to fulfillment, and before long they realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Thus, as the bodhisattva trains in the perfection of patience, gradually reaching its ultimate limit, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva thus abides in the embrace of the perfection of patience, they can endure the abuse and slander of others with a mind as immovable as Mount Sumeru; their roots of merit and virtue increase and become difficult to destroy, and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, universally bringing great benefit to the world.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"If, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing patience, two people should come before him:
one with a virtuous mind who anoints his body with sandalwood paste, and another with an evil mind who burns his body with fire."
"What kind of mind should a bodhisattva arouse toward them?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:

"This bodhisattva mahāsattva, desiring to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, should not arouse attachment toward the first person, nor should he arouse aversion toward the second person. He should arouse a mind of equanimity toward both, wishing for their ultimate benefit and happiness."
In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is able to practice the perfection of patience and is able to abide in the perfection of patience.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to practice the perfection of patience and is able to abide in the perfection of patience, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to practice the sphere of bodhisattva conduct without error and is able to dwell in the pure land of a bodhisattva without error.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not give rise to a mind of anger toward sentient beings, should not give rise to a mind of resentment, and should not give rise to a mind of seeking revenge.

In this way, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, toward the class of sentient beings, is perfected in patience, perfected in praise, perfected in gentleness, and perfected in intention; they are without anger and without resentment, giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness in all circumstances.

In this way, when other sentient beings come before these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and give rise to thoughts of enmity and malice—desiring to strike, bind, humiliate, or rebuke them—they are all able to endure with patience, having no intention to retaliate.

In this way, when other sentient beings come before these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with the intent to incite strife or cause harm, the bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of harmony and kindness, using gentle words and expressions of regret to cause their malicious intentions to subside.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected thus:
'Such sentient beings have come to me, desiring to incite strife and do me harm.'"

"When I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall proclaim the profound Dharma of emptiness to bring all strife and contention to eternal cessation. That is to say, I shall proclaim that the entire aggregate of form is like a magical illusion and is ultimately empty by nature; since there is nothing to contend over within ultimate emptiness, those who hear this will have their contentious minds stilled. Furthermore, I shall proclaim that the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all like magical illusions and are ultimately empty by nature; since there is nothing to contend over within ultimate emptiness, those who hear this will have their contentious minds stilled."

Or they proclaim that all bases of the eye are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; in ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife and quarreling are stilled. They also proclaim that all bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; in ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife and quarreling are stilled.

Or they may proclaim that all forms (*rūpāyatana*) are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is no contention within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their minds of strife. Likewise, they may proclaim that all sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is no contention within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their minds of strife.

Or they proclaim that all eye-spheres (*cakṣurdhātu*) are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is no contention within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their contentious minds. They also proclaim that all ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-spheres (*śrotra-, ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-, manodhātu*) are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is no contention within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their contentious minds.

Or they proclaim that all realms of form are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend with within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to have their contentious minds stilled. They also proclaim that all realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend with within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to have their contentious minds stilled.

Or they proclaim that all elements of visual consciousness are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty in nature; in ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife and quarreling are stilled. They also proclaim that all elements of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty in nature; in ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife and quarreling are stilled.

Or they proclaim that all visual contacts are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend with within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to have their contentious minds stilled. They likewise proclaim that all auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contacts are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend with within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to have their contentious minds stilled.

Or they proclaim that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend over within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their minds of strife. Likewise, they proclaim that all feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since there is nothing to contend over within ultimate emptiness, they cause those who hear this to pacify their minds of strife.

"Or, for the sake of proclaiming that all earth elements are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature, and that within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife may be stilled; and likewise, for the sake of proclaiming that all water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature, and that within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, so that upon hearing this, their minds of strife may be stilled."

Or they proclaim that all causes and conditions are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, those who hear this will have their contentious minds stilled. They also proclaim that all immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these various conditions are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty of intrinsic nature; since within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, those who hear this will have their contentious minds stilled.

Or, for the sake of proclaiming that all ignorance is like an illusion or a magical creation and is ultimately empty of intrinsic nature—wherein ultimate emptiness is free from all contention—he causes their contentious minds to subside upon hearing this. Furthermore, for the sake of proclaiming that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are all like illusions or magical creations and are ultimately empty of intrinsic nature—wherein ultimate emptiness is free from all contention—he causes their contentious minds to subside upon hearing this.

Or they proclaim that all realms of the desire world are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty in nature; since within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, they cause those who hear this to still their minds of strife. They also proclaim that all realms of the form world, the formless world, and the outflow-free realm are like illusions and transformations, ultimately empty in nature; since within ultimate emptiness there is no contention, they cause those who hear this to still their minds of strife.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva reflects:

'When I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, I shall teach such a Dharma to all sentient beings so that they may forever extinguish all strife and contention, their minds becoming as equanimous as space, no longer seeking out various faults or vulnerabilities in one another. By this, they shall attain a body adorned with the marks of a Great Man, which brings joy to all who see it and causes them to mutually benefit one another, until they realize the coolness of Nirvana, free from all conceptual proliferation and possessed of ultimate peace and happiness.'"
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Regarding the two kinds of patience—those of the bodhisattva and those of the śrāvaka—one should know which is more vast, subtle, pure, and supreme?"
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"I shall now question the Venerable One based on a present matter; please answer as you see fit."
Śāriputra said, “Ask whatever you wish; I shall answer for you.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Regarding the two kinds of luster—those of common iron from the world and those of Jambūnada gold—which one should be known as more vast, subtle, pure, and excellent?"
Śāriputra said:
"The luster of all the iron plowshares in the world cannot be compared to the Jambūnada gold; for the luster of Jambūnada gold is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"The patience of a śrāvaka is like the luster of ordinary iron; the patience of a bodhisattva is like the luster of Jambūnada gold. One should understand this as the distinguishing characteristic of the superiority and inferiority of these two types of patience."
Why is this? Śāriputra,

all the patience (kṣānti) possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is induced by the contemplation of the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness as being devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a soul, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.

The patience possessed by those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates that from the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness, all are devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and are brought forth from primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of Bodhisattvas is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of Śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates only the sense bases from the eye-base up to the mind-base as being devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a living being, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the sense bases from the eye-base up to the mind-base as being entirely without intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and as being primordially quiescent. Therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates only the sense bases from form (*rūpa*) up to phenomena (*dharma*), as being induced by the absence of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a mind-born being, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the sense bases from form up to phenomena, but as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and as being primordially quiescent; therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates only the eye-element up to the mind-element as being devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a soul, a human, a doer, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer; it is brought forth by these [notions].

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the eye-element up to the mind-element as being entirely without intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and brought forth by primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of a Bodhisattva is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the Śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena as being induced by the absence of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer.

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the realm of form up to the realm of phenomena as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and as being induced by primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates only the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element as being produced by what is without a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a soul, a human, a doer, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer.

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element as being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and produced from primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of Bodhisattvas is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the Śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle consists solely in observing that from eye-contact through to mind-contact, there is no self, sentient being, life-force, soul, nourisher, person, individual, mind-born, youth, agent, experiencer, knower, or seer; it is brought forth by these [notions].

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise observes that from eye-contact through to mind-contact, they are entirely without intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and are brought forth by primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of Bodhisattvas is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the Śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle consists solely in contemplating that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a creature, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a soul, a human, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer; it is merely brought forth by these [conditions].

The patience possessed by those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle also contemplates that all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition, up to and including all feelings produced with mind-contact as a condition, are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; they are without arising and without cessation, without defilement and without purification, without increase and without decrease, and are brought forth from primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience possessed by Bodhisattvas is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience possessed by Śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is that which contemplates only the earth element up to the consciousness element as being incited by the absence of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a soul, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer.

The patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise contemplates the earth element up to the consciousness element as being entirely without intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and incited by primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of a bodhisattva is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of the śrāvakas.

The patience possessed by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle observes only that everything from ignorance up to old age and death is brought forth by what is devoid of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer;

the patience possessed by those of the Bodhisattva vehicle likewise observes that everything from ignorance up to old age and death is entirely without intrinsic nature, without arising or cessation, without defilement or purity, without increase or decrease, and is brought forth by primordial tranquility. Therefore, the patience of Bodhisattvas is vast, subtle, pure, and supreme, surpassing all the patience of Śrāvakas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and if an enemy or thief comes to sever their limbs and joints, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
'The number of grains of sand in the Ganges River may be known, but the number of bodies [one has taken] is difficult to know.'"
Since both the body that is the object of cognition and the cognizer are comprised of matter (*rūpa*), their constituent parts are difficult to discern;
as for the parts of the body that are the objects of cognition, they are extremely few—how could anger possibly arise on account of them?

"Thus, when this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates such meaning, even if they encounter hostile bandits who dismember their limbs, they are able to endure it, harboring no anger, resentment, or malice whatsoever."
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, according to the mind of patience they have generated, dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes, thereby embracing the perfection of patience.
In this way, it should be known that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never at any time abandons the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and someone comes to strike or revile them, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:

"The sands of the Ganges River may have their quantity known, but the faults of my own body are difficult to know; namely, the various afflictions and evil karmas initiated since beginningless time which contradict and harm principle and phenomena, and which are collectively censured and rejected by all Buddhas and noble sages."

Now, this person comes to beat and revile me; yet even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a fraction as small as an *upaniṣad*, does not equal one part of my [merit]. How could I, on account of this, give rise to anger?
"By contemplating this meaning, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to endure being struck or reviled by others, remaining entirely free from anger, resentment, or malice."
These bodhisattva mahāsattvas, in accordance with the mind of patience they have generated, dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes, thereby embracing the perfection of patience.
In this way, it should be known that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never, at any time, abandons the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and if enemies or bandits come to plunder their wealth and treasures, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"The nature of such wealth and treasures is entirely empty and belongs to nothing; how could I give rise to anger on account of them?"

When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates such meanings, even if they encounter enemies or bandits who plunder their wealth and treasures, their mind remains entirely free from anger, resentment, or malice.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, according to the mind of patience they have generated, dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes and thereby embrace the perfection of patience.
In this way, it should be known that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never at any time abandons the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should cultivate their mind so that it accords with earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth.
Śāriputra asked:
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening cultivate his mind so that it accords with earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

“If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should cultivate their minds so that they are like the great earth, great water, great fire, great wind, and space—free from all conceptual discrimination.”
Śāriputra asked:

"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening cultivate his mind so that it is like the great earth, free from all conceptual discrimination?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"For example, although desirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast upon the great earth, it does not give rise to any elation, joy, or attachment;
and although undesirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast upon it, it does not give rise to any depression, grief, or resentment."
In this way, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters various desirable objects of perception, they should not give rise to elation, joy, or attachment;
and although they encounter various undesirable conditions, they should not give rise to dejection, sorrow, or resentment.

Patience and pure faith are constantly present before them, revolving with impartiality like the great earth; therefore, it is said that the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate their minds so that they are like the great earth, free from all discrimination.
Śāriputra asked:
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment cultivate his mind so that it is like great water, free from all discrimination?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"It is like a great body of water: although one might cast into it desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, it does not give rise to any exaltation, joy, or attachment;
and although one might cast into it undesirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, it does not give rise to any depression, grief, or resentment."
In this way, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters various desirable objects of perception, they should not give rise to elation, delight, or attachment;
and although they encounter various undesirable conditions, they should not give rise to dejection, sorrow, or resentment.

Patience and pure faith are constantly present before them, flowing with impartiality like a great body of water; therefore, it is said that the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate their minds so that they are like great water, free from all discrimination.
Śāriputra asked:
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening cultivate his mind so that it is like a great fire, free from all conceptual discrimination?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“It is, for example, like a great fire: even if one throws desirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles into it, it does not give rise to any high joy, delight, or affection;
and even if one throws undesirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles into it, it does not give rise to any low dejection, sorrow, or resentment.”
In this way, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas encounter various desirable objects of perception, they should not give rise to elation, joy, or attachment;
and although they encounter various undesirable conditions, they should not give rise to dejection, sorrow, or resentment.

Patience and pure faith are constantly present before them, evolving with equanimity like a great fire; therefore, it is said that the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate their minds so that they are like a great fire, free from all conceptual discrimination.
Śāriputra asked:
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva, who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, cultivate his mind so that it is like a great wind, free from all conceptual discrimination?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"For example, it is like a great wind: even if pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast into it, it gives rise to no sense of elation, joy, or attachment;
and even if unpleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast into it, it gives rise to no sense of dejection, sorrow, or resentment."
In this way, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas encounter various desirable objects of perception, they should not give rise to elation, joy, or attachment;
and although they encounter various undesirable conditions, they should not give rise to dejection, sorrow, or resentment.

Patience and pure faith are constantly present before them, moving with impartiality like a great wind; therefore, it is said that the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate their minds so that they are like a great wind, free from all conceptual discrimination.
Śāriputra asked:
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment cultivate his mind so that it is like space, free from all conceptual discrimination?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"For example, it is like space: even if desirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast into it, it does not give rise to any elation, joy, or attachment;
nor, even if undesirable forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are cast into it, does it give rise to any depression, sorrow, or resentment."
In this way, although bodhisattva-mahāsattvas encounter various desirable objects of perception, they should not give rise to elation, delight, or attachment;
and although they encounter various undesirable conditions, they should not give rise to dejection, sorrow, or resentment.

Patience and pure faith are constantly present before them, evolving with equanimity like space; therefore, it is said that the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate their minds so that they are non-conceptual, like space.
Then, Śāriputra asked the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Since space is unconditioned, are the bodhisattvas not also subsumed within the unconditioned?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"The assembly of bodhisattvas is not subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Rather, through their skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), bodhisattvas contemplate body and mind as being equal to space, such that they do not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding objects. Thus they become capable of practicing the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*); that is to say, through their skillful means, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplate body and mind as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unimpeded, and equal to space, thereby becoming able to endure various contacts such as those from blades and staves."

In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through their skillful means and relying upon the perfection of wisdom, contemplate the body and mind as being equal to space; they embrace the perfection of patience, such that even if they were constantly oppressed by the fierce fires of hell, the blades and clubs of hell, and other instruments of torture, they would still be able to endure them, their minds remaining equanimous, unmoving, and unchanging.

In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practices the perfection of wisdom and embraces the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate their own bodies and minds as being equal to space; thus, they are able to endure all sufferings without wavering or changing. That this assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can endure all sufferings without wavering or changing is itself the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner, upon encountering severe suffering, they form this thought:

"Since beginningless saṃsāra, although I have experienced intense physical and mental sufferings, by means of such suffering I have not yet been able to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or even the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; how much less could I realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through such suffering!"

Since the various sufferings currently experienced by my body and mind will certainly lead me to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, I should now accept them with joy.

"In this way, because the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas contemplates this meaning, although they undergo manifold sufferings, they are able to give rise to a superior, intense, and keen joy and endure them with patience."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For example, suppose there is a person who eats food of a hundred flavors, and his body and mind become refreshed and joyful, giving rise to supreme delight.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva sees a beggar come—whether seeking wealth and resources, or seeking his own limbs and body, or undergoing various sufferings for the sake of practicing generosity—he joyfully endures them with his body and mind becoming refreshed and joyful; this surpasses the previous refreshment by many hundreds of thousands of times."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Just as when an arhat beholds a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, although his outflows are already exhausted, he gives rise to a mind of extraordinary faith, reverence, and joy.

In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas sees a petitioner come to seek either material wealth or their own body parts, they give rise to a mind of supreme faith, reverence, and joy; they are able to deeply endure the various heavy sufferings inflicted by that person, such as harm, abuse, and slander. At the very moment they arouse a mind of patience, they dedicate [the merit] toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gives rise to a mind of patience, they dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes; they never depart from the perfection of patience they have cultivated, and they constantly and uninterruptedly bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate patience toward all sentient beings. They should not strike back when struck, nor respond with abuse when abused, nor respond with slander when slandered, nor respond with anger when angered, nor respond with reproach when reproached, nor respond with resentment when resentful, nor respond with wrath when provoked to wrath, nor respond with harm when harmed; they must be able to endure all such evil deeds."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never abandon the mind of omniscience, desiring to bring benefit to all sentient beings.

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never abandon the mind of omniscience and desire to bring benefit to all sentient beings, even if their bodies were pierced by hundreds of thousands of spears and javelins, they would not harbor a single thought of retaliation or malice, but would always maintain pure faith and patient endurance toward them.

In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) and desires to bring benefit to all sentient beings, they will certainly obtain a body of true golden color, adorned with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), which brings joy to all who behold it.
"Therefore, Śāriputra,
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should all diligently cultivate the power of patience, enduring all sufferings such as those inflicted by harm."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the power of patience and endures all sufferings, thereby embracing the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), that bodhisattva mahāsattva remains far removed from birth and death while drawing near to omniscience (sarvajñatā), and is able to bring great benefit to sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva takes delight in the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from the bodhisattva perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).

Why is this? Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas would rather personally undergo the boundless great suffering of birth and death than become attached to the various merits of self-benefit characteristic of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes attached to the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, it should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has fallen away from his own sphere of practice and is practicing the sphere of others.
Then, Śāriputra asked the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the conduct of others?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the path of others;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva gives rise to the mental orientation of a śrāvaka or the mental orientation of a pratyekabuddha, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the path of others;

if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes pleasure in and clings to the teachings associated with the śrāvakas, or takes pleasure in discourse associated with the pratyekabuddhas, that bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the path of others."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the aggregate of form as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the aggregate of form as either pleasant or painful, and contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pleasant or painful, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the aggregate of form as either self or non-self, and contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the aggregate of form as either pure or impure, and contemplates the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the path of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the sense-base of the eye as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the sense base of the eye as either pleasant or painful, and contemplates the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pleasant or painful, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the sense base of the eye as either self or non-self, and contemplates the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' practices.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the sense base of the eye as either pure or impure, and contemplates the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the path of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the sphere of forms as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the sense base of forms as either pleasant or painful, and contemplates the sense bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as either pleasant or painful, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the sense-sphere of form as either self or non-self, and contemplates the sense-spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the sphere of forms as either pure or impure, and contemplates the spheres of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the path of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-element as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-element as either pleasant or painful, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements as either pleasant or painful, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-element as either self or non-self, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' practices.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-element as either pure or impure, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-elements as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the realm of form as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the realm of form as either pleasure or pain, and contemplates the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as either pleasure or pain, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the realm of form as either self or non-self, and contemplates the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the realm of form as either pure or impure, and contemplates the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the path of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-consciousness element as either permanent or impermanent, and contemplates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements as either permanent or impermanent, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the way of others."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the eye-consciousness element as either pleasant or painful, and contemplates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements as either pleasant or painful, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates the eye-consciousness element as either self or non-self, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements as either self or non-self, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' practices.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the eye-consciousness element as either pure or impure, and contemplates the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements as either pure or impure, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva is practicing the sphere of others' conduct.
Then, Śāriputra again asked the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice his own sphere of activity?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections with a mental orientation associated with the knowledge of all modes, this is the domain of practice for that bodhisattva mahāsattva."
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, no evil māras will be able to find an opportunity.
Just as a jackal cannot find an opportunity against turtles or tortoises, and because it finds no opportunity, its movements are free and unimpeded.
In this way, when the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practices the six perfections, no evil māras can find an opportunity; because they cannot find an opportunity, their conduct is sovereign.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose that Māra, the Evil One, were to universally transform all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm into evil Māras, and each of these Māras were to have as many demonic armies and retinues as there are beings, surrounding them from front and back as they approach the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells."
When these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the six perfections, those evil māras are unable to find an opportunity; because they find no opportunity, their conduct is sovereign and unimpeded.
For example, a jackal finds no opportunity against tortoises or turtles; because it finds no opportunity, its movements are free and unimpeded.
"Therefore, Śāriputra! [he said].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way:
"My mind must not be separated from the six perfections.
If the mind is not separated from these six perfections, no evil Māras will be able to find an opportunity; because they cannot find an opportunity, their conduct will be sovereign.
Then, Śāriputra again asked the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand all demonic activities as they truly are?”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in hearing the teachings corresponding to the pāramitās, you should know that this is the work of evil māras."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in receiving and upholding the teachings corresponding to the pāramitās, you should know that this is the work of evil māras.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in reading and reciting the teachings associated with the pāramitās, you should know that this is the work of Māras.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in contemplating the teachings associated with the pāramitās, you should know that this is the work of Māras.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not delight in practicing the dharmas associated with the perfections (pāramitā), you should know that this is the work of evil māras.
Having realized this matter, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reflect as follows:

"This must certainly be the skillful means of an evil Māra to obstruct my mind's pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna). I should not now follow his desires, but should instead diligently practice and study the perfections (pāramitā)."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva should not feel anger toward that evil Māra, nor should they give rise to a mind of intolerance; practicing in this way constitutes the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
This bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:

"When I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall preach for sentient beings the Dharma that can forever sever greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, I should not feel anger toward that evil Māra now."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains such mindfulness, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva surpasses all evil Māras and practices with mastery the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
If at any time the mental engagement associated with the knowledge of all modes does not manifest before a bodhisattva mahāsattva, at that time the bodhisattva mahāsattva should form this thought:
"I must not now act in an improper manner, causing me to lose mindfulness of the knowledge of all modes."
"In this way, a bodhisattva should reproach himself, thinking:
'I am now wasting my time in vain.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
“What constitutes the wasting of time?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied,

“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices any one of these six perfections but fails to bring to mind the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and fails to dedicate it toward the knowledge of all modes, that bodhisattva mahāsattva wastes his time and diminishes the fruit of his time.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing any one of these six perfections, is able to recollect the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and dedicate it toward the knowledge of all modes on either the second or the third day, then although this bodhisattva mahāsattva has committed an offense, they are said to possess the fruit of occasional [practice].
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"What is the difference between the patience of a bodhisattva and the patience possessed by an arhat?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"I now ask the Venerable One:
what is the difference between Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and a small mustard seed—in terms of their size, height, and weight?"
Śāriputra said: "There are immeasurable distinctions.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“The patience of a bodhisattva and the patience possessed by an arhat are likewise; thus, this should not be a subject for questioning.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, what do you think?”
"Between the water in the great ocean and the water on the tip of a single hair,
which is more? Śāriputra replied,
"The water in the great ocean and the water on the tip of a single hair cannot be compared in their quantity, even by way of a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even an *upaniṣad* part."
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

“The patience of a bodhisattva and the patience possessed by an arhat are likewise; even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even an upaniṣad-part cannot compare to their relative magnitude. Therefore, one should not ask such a question.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.
You have well explained the perfection of patience by relying on the Buddha’s power.

However, if one were to grasp at the magnitude of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s patience and compare it with the patience of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one would be grasping at the magnitude of the Tathāgata’s patience and comparing it with the patience of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
"Why is this? The measure of the patience accomplished by the assembly of bodhisattvas is boundless; it should not be compared with the patience of śrāvakas and the like.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold the perfection of patience practiced by the bodhisattva mahāsattvas as taught by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; do not let it be forgotten or lost!"
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
I have already received and upheld the perfection of patience practiced by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as taught by the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; I shall certainly never forget it!

When the Blessed One had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Ānanda, as well as the other śrāvakas, the assembly of bodhisattvas, and all others—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and so forth—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle Five Hundred and Eighty-nine.
